That doesn't affect it's use in a specific case, and compilers just use the instructions that they are programmed to use, so there isn't anything fundamentally wrong with this instruction or it's name other than the fact that it seems to be a key for a lock.If there were more people programming in asm, there would probably be enough minds interacting with the instructions to desire and have the capacity to design a better representation for the instruction set.  I do believe that better designs at levels like that help solidify thinking in neighbouring levels.  For instance with instruction representations, a better way to think about how the instruction is specified might reduce the cognitive load on chip designers and compiler writers.This kind of thing happens over and over when people move to new methods, there are artifacts that remain that are still useful in a modern context but only exist because they were designed at a time when the principles that underlying them were much more commonly used.Examples of this are music boxes and regular expressions, You can still find new instances for both, and they are good solutions for some tasks, but if anyone were to design something today to fill the niche of either, they would not come up with anything so enduring.It is easier to understand a music box than a regular expression finite automata, but both are wonders of design.It has occurred to me that this specific problem of ideas and methods left unconsidered may not be such a problem in an age of AI.  It mY be that the capacity for AI to consider and link so many things that it will draw together elements from all of those domains to apply techniques that humans no longer focus upon onto issues that are currently relevant.I'm not sure if current AI is up to that particular task. You're assuming that the asm syntax is targeted at human readability, when it's at least as much to ease the complexity of the assembler and disassembler.If the FMA instruction syntax was designed for readability, then it would have used 4-argument syntax with a requirement for two registers to match instead of using the 1/2/3 encodings. But the reason why it uses those names instead is that it's more consistent with the instruction encoding and the format of most other vector instructions: the register/memory argument is last.Similarly, x86 vector instructions that take an immediate byte cram a bunch of options into that byte, such as shuffle masks or operation options. The assembly syntax does not help constructing this byte at all. But that's because it's meant to map straightforwardly to the instruction encoding, not to be easy to manually read or write.ARM assembly tends to be a bit more consistent, but has some similar quirks. The majority of ARM instructions are dst,src, but store instructions are reversed as src,dst so they have the memory argument second just like load instructions.reply

So there's a constant need for new prints of most of these tools. The ones that are more durable, the cell has to be more careful to not overproduce.)I say that "tool blueprints" is a useful model, because it makes it more intuitive that e.g. for the important stuff, the genome keeps a pile of duplicate blueprints for the same tool; and then also keeps some machinery (autosense suppressors) to add and remove notes to those blueprints on observing that there's "enough" or "not enough" of the tool floating around inside/outside the cell. Which allows "having N redundant tool blueprints" to work just like "having only one tool blueprint" does, rather than drowning you in printed tools; yet also ensures that if something scribbles over one of the blueprints, everything "just keeps working", since the machinery will just end up unsilencing the other blueprints more often. (And also, as a bonus, allows the "corrupted" duplicate blueprints to act as forks of the parent blueprint, gradually being redrawn over N generations of mutations into a working blueprint for a new tool, much more quickly than a new tool blueprint could be mutated into existence from scratch, and without losing the ability to produce the original tool in the process.)---Oh, and to be even more pedantic, it's probably best to think of genes as tool part blueprints, since several proteins might need to come together and link up to make a functional tool; and since a single part might end up being consumed in the creation of several different tools.
